summaries.example: Think about a cat and a mat. “Black” describes the cat by itself, so black is a property. “On top of” connects the cat and the mat, so it is a relation. Some relations have an order: the cat is on top of the mat, but the mat is not on top of the cat. Other relations are shared both ways: if Mia is next to Leo, Leo is next to Mia.
summaries.summary: A relation is a connection between things. “Being a cat” or “being black” is usually treated as a property: it belongs to one thing. “Being beside,” “being inside,” or “being taller than” connects one thing with another, so it is a relation. Relations may involve two things or more. They may also behave differently. “Next to” is symmetric because the connection goes both ways. “Taller than” is non-symmetric because its order matters. Philosophers ask whether relations must be added to our picture of reality, or whether some relations can be explained using only the things and properties involved. They also ask how an ordered connection can work. One proposal says that a relation has a direction, like an arrow. Other proposals use positions, patterns among many related facts, or treat the order as something basic that cannot be explained further. The entry presents these ideas as an ongoing debate rather than a settled answer.
key_ideas: Properties describe things, while relations connect things.
Relations can involve two things, three things, or more.
Some relations work both ways; others have an important order.
Philosophers disagree about whether relations are real things, whether some can be explained by properties, and how order in relations works.
Science often describes the world using relations, including distance and connections between physical things.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relations appear in ordinary life, mathematics, and science. They help us describe where things are, how things compare, and how events or objects are connected. Thinking carefully about relations also teaches us to notice the difference between a thing’s own features and the ways things are linked. That difference can affect what we think the world is made of.

important_terms.definition: A feature something has by itself, such as being black, round, or tall.
A connection that holds between two or more things, such as being next to or taller than.
A relation involving exactly two things.
A relation that works the same way in either direction, such as being next to.
A relation whose direction matters, such as being above or taller than.

questions_to_think_about: Is “being red” different from “being next to the door”? Why?
Can something have a relation with itself?
Why does “above” seem different from “next to”?
If two things have different heights, do we also need a relation called “taller than”?
Why might scientists need relations in their descriptions?

summaries.example: Suppose a metal ball is one meter from a magnet. The ball’s mass and shape may be properties of the ball, while its distance from the magnet is a relation involving the ball and the magnet. A philosopher might ask whether that distance is an additional feature of reality, or whether it is fixed by the intrinsic features of the objects and their larger physical setting. The question becomes more difficult in modern physics, where quantities may depend on fields, spacetime structure, or the scale of description.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what relations are and what philosophical work they do. It begins by contrasting properties, which are normally one-place features, with relations, which connect two or more relata. Relations can have different arities and can be symmetric, non-symmetric, or asymmetric. A non-symmetric relation is order-sensitive: “A loves B” does not entail “B loves A,” while “A is adjacent to B” does entail its reverse. The entry then considers internal and external relations. Different accounts define internality through necessity, the intrinsic natures of the relata, or supervenience. Some philosophers therefore try to reduce internal relations to properties of the relata. The entry argues that this move must distinguish truth-makers—what makes a claim true—from ontological commitments—what the claim quantifies over or refers to. It also notes challenges from physics, including field theories, relativity, and quantum entanglement, which complicate the idea that fundamental features are purely intrinsic. Bradley’s regress is a major objection to external relations: if a relation must itself be related to its relata, an endless series seems to follow. Proposed responses appeal to facts or relation-specific tropes, though the entry notes that these may presuppose the very relational capacity at issue. Finally, the entry studies how non-symmetric relations produce order. Directionalism explains this through a relation’s direction, while positionalist, anti-positionalist, and primitivist accounts explain or accept order in different ways. No single approach is presented as decisively established.
key_ideas: Relations differ from properties because they connect relata rather than merely characterizing one item.
Relations can be classified by arity, symmetry, and whether reversing their relata changes their application.
The internal–external distinction has several versions, involving necessity, intrinsic properties, or supervenience.
Bradley’s regress challenges the intelligibility of external relations by asking how a relation relates its relata without requiring another relation.
Reductionists argue that internal relations may add nothing to reality beyond the relata and their properties, but critics distinguish truth-makers from ontological commitments.
The nature of order in non-symmetric relations remains disputed. Directionalism, positionalism, anti-positionalism, and primitivism offer different approaches.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relations are central to metaphysics because they influence what counts as a thing, a property, a fact, and a basic feature of the world. They are also important for understanding scientific theories: distance, motion, fields, and quantum entanglement may resist simple descriptions in terms of isolated objects and intrinsic properties. The debate shows how apparently ordinary phrases such as “next to,” “taller than,” or “causes” raise deep questions about explanation, existence, and structure.

important_terms.definition: A feature exhibited by one thing, considered as a one-place characteristic.
A connection borne by one thing to another or to several other things.
The number of places or participants required by a relation; a binary relation has two, while a ternary relation has three.
A relation that has the same truth in either order: if x bears it to y, y bears it to x.
A relation for which reversing the relata changes the relation’s application; an asymmetric relation also rules out its reverse holding.
A relation whose holding is fixed by the existence or intrinsic character of its relata, in one of several philosophical senses.
A relation not fixed in that way by the relata taken separately; spatial distance is discussed as a possible example.
The relation obtained by reversing the order of a binary relation: the converse of “above” is “below.”

questions_to_think_about: Can a relation be real even if its holding is fully determined by the properties of its relata?
Does explaining a statement’s truth explain what the statement is about?
Does Bradley’s regress show that relations are unintelligible, or does it misuse the idea of relating?
Is a converse relation a second relation, or merely another way of describing one state?
Should the structure of modern physics make us cautious about reducing relations to intrinsic properties?

summaries.example: Imagine two students, Ava and Ben, standing in line. “Ava is wearing a blue shirt” describes Ava alone, so it is about a property. “Ava is before Ben” connects Ava and Ben, so it is about a relation. This relation is not symmetric: if Ava is before Ben, Ben is not before Ava. But “Ava is next to Ben” is usually symmetric. A philosopher might then ask whether “before” is a real connection, or whether it can be explained entirely by facts about the students, the line, and their positions.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of relations asks how things are connected and whether those connections belong in our account of reality. A property, such as being blue, is normally treated as a feature of one thing. A relation, such as being next to or taller than, involves one thing in connection with another. Relations can have different arities: “between” involves three things, while “next to” involves two. They also differ in symmetry. If Ava is next to Ben, Ben is next to Ava; but if Ava is taller than Ben, the reverse does not follow. The entry examines several further distinctions. Internal relations are fixed by the relata or by their intrinsic natures, while external relations are not fixed in that way. Some philosophers use this to argue that internal relations can be reduced to properties. Critics reply that what makes a statement true is not always the same as what the statement commits us to existing. The entry also discusses Bradley’s regress, an argument claiming that a relation would need another relation to connect it to its relata, leading to an endless chain. Proposed solutions include facts and particular relation-like entities, but these proposals are debated. A final issue is order: how can “A loves B” differ from “B loves A”? Some theories appeal to direction, others to argument positions or patterns among related states, and primitivists treat this difference as basic. The entry maps these disagreements without presenting one final solution.
key_ideas: Properties describe individual things, while relations connect things.
A relation may involve a fixed number of participants, though philosophers debate whether some relations can vary in number.
Symmetry concerns whether switching the things changes the result.
Some philosophers think relations are unnecessary additions because properties of the relata already settle the relational facts.
Other philosophers argue that relations may still matter even when they help explain why a claim is true rather than making it true by themselves.
Bradley’s regress and the debate about direction show why explaining relations is difficult.
summaries.why_it_matters: Relations help us describe comparisons, positions, sequences, causes, and connections. They also reveal that ordinary grammar can hide difficult assumptions. Asking whether “before,” “distance,” or “greater than” is a real relation can change how we understand objects and scientific theories. Studying the debate is useful practice in comparing arguments and separating questions about truth from questions about what exists.

important_terms.definition: A characteristic that belongs to one thing, such as being blue or being tall.
A connection that holds between things, such as being before, next to, or inside.
How many places a relation has. “Next to” has two places; “between” has three.
A relation that holds in both directions when it holds in one, such as “is next to.”
A relation whose order matters. A special kind, asymmetric, cannot hold in both directions at once.
A relation whose holding depends in some important way on the things related or on their intrinsic features.
A relation whose holding is not fixed by the relata considered separately in that way.
The reversed form of a relation. The converse of “before” is “after.”

questions_to_think_about: Is “being taller than” just a result of two heights, or is there also a real relation?
Why is “next to” symmetric but “before” non-symmetric?
Would a relation still exist if nothing happened to have it?
Does adding another relation really solve Bradley’s regress?
Can two descriptions use different relations but point to the same situation?
